review.material: Author-hosted April 2013 prepublication draft: introductory complexity discussion and §4, especially §4.2 on parametric subshape recognition.
review.limitations: Locators refer to the 43-page draft, not the journal pagination. Reduction arguments were read but not independently proved. The paper’s use of NP terminology needs the qualification below.

sections.title: In brief
sections.text: This paper investigates why unrestricted shape computation can become computationally difficult and what restrictions make useful practical algorithms possible. Parametric recognition is a central example.

sections.title: The question
sections.text: Which difficulties arise from the full expressive power of grammars, and which arise when searching for parameters that make a rule match a particular shape?

sections.title: Main idea or claim
sections.text: General shape grammars can simulate unrestricted computation, so general termination or language-membership procedures cannot simply be assumed. Parametric matching can also require a rapidly growing search.

sections.title: How the work approaches it
sections.text: The authors formalize grammar mechanisms, relate their expressive power to Turing computation, and analyze parametric subshape recognition through problem reductions and enumeration of parameter assignments.

sections.title: Evidence and examples
sections.text: The support is computational argument and worked constructions, including a reduction involving clique. The paper discusses the number of possible assignments rather than presenting a user study or a current hardware benchmark.

sections.title: What comes out of it
sections.text: A search on n candidate points with k independent choices can grow like n^k. Holding k fixed gives a polynomial bound in n for that enumeration; allowing k to grow changes the conclusion. Restrictions on parameters and rules therefore matter.

sections.title: Limits to keep in mind
sections.text: The draft sometimes uses NP loosely when arguing hardness. Membership in NP alone does not imply intractability, and P ≠ NP is not proved. Its argument should not be quoted as settling that open problem or guaranteeing that every small grammar is fast.

sections.title: What to take from it
sections.text: Distinguish worst-case complexity from practical limits. A finite menu, bounded parameters or a restricted grammar can make exploration usable, but its scope must remain visible.
